# CLAUDE.md — Klide project context

This file is loaded automatically when Claude Code works in this directory. Read it first.

## What Klide is

Klide is a code editor Pierre is building from scratch. The goal is a small, fast, AI-first IDE that **looks like a 2026 design tool**, **works like a full-featured code editor**, and **treats agents as a first-class surface** — an editor and an agentic control panel in one shell.

Pierre is new to building desktop apps and is learning Rust as he goes. Frame technical explanations for a smart beginner — explain what each piece does, cite docs, and prefer fewer-moving-parts solutions.

## Vision in one sentence

**A familiar IDE structure, a calm minimal aesthetic, and fluent AI — Tauri-light, local-model-first, agent-native.**

## Design philosophy

"Minimalist" here is a **visual/UX principle**, not a feature-pruning principle.

| ✅ Do | ❌ Don't |
|---|---|
| Keep the familiar IDE structural layout (sidebar rail, tabs, editor, status bar, panel) | Strip out structural elements to "simplify" |
| Quiet light/dark palettes with shared app + terminal tokens | Saturated accent colors, gradients, drop shadows |
| Generous whitespace, rounded groups, thin borders and subtle panel shadows | Heavy frames, dividers or shadows |
| Restrained type — San Francisco for macOS UI, Inter for wordmark, Monaspace for code | Multiple display fonts, decorative weights |
| Subtle, considered motion (fades, no bounces) | Springy animations |
| Icons only when they earn their place | Icon-for-every-button maximalism |

If a UI element doesn't serve clarity, it doesn't ship.

### App-wide palette and shape

Use **very light cool grey #F5F6F7 for chrome, rails and sidebars** and
**white #FFFFFF for content, editor, terminal and panel surfaces** throughout
all light themes. No beige, cream, parchment or warm off-white UI backgrounds.
Use the shared tokens in `src/styles/tokens.css`, and keep Monaco colours,
terminal colours, viewer surfaces and theme swatches in sync with them. Dark
themes keep their dark surfaces; user content, artwork and service logos retain
their own colours.

Group related settings in rounded panels (20px corners), with generous row
spacing, fine dividers and rounded controls (12px). Use subtle chevrons for
functional dropdowns or expandable groups; use full arrows for directional
navigation. Omit decorative trailing icons and browser triangle markers.
Page titles stand alone by default; subtitles are optional and must add useful
context. Put guidance beside the control it explains.
`CONTEXT.md` and `Design.md` document these approved guidelines.


## Stack

| Layer | Tech | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| Shell | **Tauri 2** | Rust backend, native webview, 27 MB app bundle (measured 2026-08-24; re-measure with `du -sh src-tauri/target/release/bundle/macos/Klide.app`) |
| Editor | **Monaco** via `@monaco-editor/react` | The browser editor core (also used by VS Code) |
| Terminal | **xterm.js** + Rust **portable-pty** | Real shell, not a sandbox |
| Frontend | **React 19 + TypeScript + Vite** | |
| Local AI | **Ollama** (`localhost:11434`) + **MLX** (`mlx_lm.server` on `:8080`) | Both run the full tool harness; default `llama3.1:8b` |
| Online AI | Anthropic, OpenAI, Mistral, xAI, DeepSeek, OpenRouter, Gemini, Vertex AI, Bedrock, Azure OpenAI, Groq, Cerebras, Fireworks, Hugging Face, Vercel AI Gateway, Cloudflare AI Gateway, Moonshot, Kimi For Coding, MiniMax, Z.AI, Xiaomi MiMo, Prime Inference + self-hosted OpenAI-wire endpoints | Keys in macOS Keychain; self-hosted tokens via `${VAR}` refs; account-scoped URLs (Azure resource, AWS region, Cloudflare account, GCP project) fill `${VAR}` from Settings / env |
| Documents | **IronCalc** (Rust) recalculates, **ExcelJS** renders | A run writes a real `.xlsx`; Klide opens it in a built-in sheet surface |
| Auto-install | `npx skills add <owner/repo>` | Skill install + uninstall via Rust commands |

## Architecture

### Three surfaces, one state

Klide opens on the surface that matches the task; all three share the same
runs, transcripts, conversations, and review state.

- **Welcome** (`WelcomeScreen.tsx`) — start or resume a project: recents,
  clone, new project.
- **Focus** (`FocusMode.tsx`) — chat-first fullscreen: one centered
  conversation (an `AiPanel` `variant="focus"`, never a duplicate chat
  implementation), a Git island, and the shared terminal docked
  *under* the canvas so run subscriptions keep streaming while you shell.
  Its picker offers every provider the workbench does — **delegate CLIs
  included**, so a Claude Code or Codex subscription can start a Focus
  conversation without an API key anywhere in Klide.
- **Workbench** (`AnchoredWorkbench.tsx`) — the editor-first IDE layout, plus
  free-mode floating panels, fixed presets, and the grid builder.

The sidebar is one `WorkspaceRail`, rendered once by `App.tsx` for every
surface — Focus included, so switching mode morphs the foot icon and leaves the
column standing rather than remounting it. Focus differs only in the `nav` and the
conversation handlers.

## Working conventions

- **Two halves, two languages.** Frontend = TypeScript/React in `src/`. Backend = Rust in `src-tauri/`. They talk via `invoke()` (request/reply), `Channel<T>` (request-scoped streaming), and `emit`/`listen` (global events).
- **The Rust harness is the agent run module.** AiPanel starts runs and renders events; it does not run its own tool loop. All modes (Plan, Work = `goal`, and the `chat` collapse) go through `startAgentRun()`.
- **No API keys in the frontend.** Provider keys live in macOS Keychain (`keyring` crate), never in localStorage or React state.
- **Workspace-rooted file access.** Agent tools verify paths are inside the workspace before reading/writing.
- **Tools are defined once in Rust.** The `ToolEntry` struct bundles schema, kind, and execution together. Frontend fetches schemas over IPC. The transcript records each call's *capability* at dispatch time — readers never guess trust effects from a tool's name.
- **Durable state goes through `durable.rs`.** Missions and Transcripts use atomic replace + flushed appends; a reader must never see a torn document, and interior corruption is an error, not a `continue`.
- **Blocking work goes through `blocking.rs`.** A sync `#[tauri::command]` runs on the main thread and an inline `std::fs`/`Command` call holds a tokio worker, so IO-bearing commands are `async fn` whose body runs in `blocking::run`, and the Harness dispatches read-only Tools through the same door. `every_sync_command_is_on_the_allowlist` in `lib.rs` fails on a new sync command nobody vouched for.
- **Icons come from `src/icons.tsx`.** One vocabulary, one weight lever; don't draw a private copy of a glyph in a component (provider/brand/file marks are the hand-drawn exception).
- **GitHub identity is pinned.** Klide applies the account from `~/.klide/github_account.json` per-command via `GH_TOKEN`; it never follows or mutates gh's global active account.
- **Styling: inline styles for now.** No CSS framework before v1.0. CSS custom properties in `src/styles/tokens.css` for theming.

A local-first coding workspace for macOS.

## One workspace for every coding agent Bring Claude Code, Codex, OpenCode, Hermes and other supported agents into one workspace alongside local models and hosted APIs. Keep your editor, terminals, conversations and change review together. - **See the work.** Follow active runs, tool calls and terminal output. # Design feedback — seven production-panel scenarios

This development-only fixture renders the **production `AiPanel`**, including
its real transcript, tool fold, message actions, scroll behavior and composer.
It uses synthetic history and an explicit native IPC mock. It does not open real
conversations, use credentials, read workspace files, or contact model providers.
No production component was copied or changed for the fixtures.

Implemented scenarios:

| Scenario | Captured states and behavior |
| --- | --- |
| `conversation-long` | Latest/earlier history; tool fold, internal code scroll and jump to latest |
| `compose-empty` | Empty composer; typing enables Send and clearing disables it |
| `tools-and-review` | Pending command, mixed tool output, proposed/expanded Diff, rejected edit |
| `waiting-and-error` | Keyboard answer, retryable provider error, recovered reply and cancelled question |
| `subagent-activity` | Running/completed/failed/stopped children, nested steps, collapsed and settled tray |
| `composer-menu` | Open picker, keyboard model selection, filtered list, Escape and focus return |
| `result-and-diff` | Three-file review run (README approved, Validate all on notes/a.md, notes/b.md auto-applied): reviewed labels, See changes opens only the unread file, compact wrapped diff, one scroll with a pinned row, reviewed file still opens |

The live scenarios replay typed synthetic Agent events through the production
Run controller. Card answers use the real IPC adapters; a development-only mock
records them, appends synthetic resolutions and emits normal Run notifications.
Retry uses the real start-Run channel; no Harness/provider/CLI is launched.
Child activity uses the normal observed-event fold and production tray. The
menu opens through its actual trigger and keeps real keyboard/focus behavior.
A development-only native visual reviewer is available; see below.
This is not a shipped Design capability or council.

## Use

Requires Node 22.12+ (the pinned accessibility dependency), `npm ci`, and a
one-time developer browser installation:

```sh
npx playwright install chromium
npm run design:capture -- --scenario conversation-long --output artifacts/design-feedback/baseline
npm run design:capture -- --scenario conversation-long --output artifacts/design-feedback/candidate
npm run design:compare -- --baseline artifacts/design-feedback/baseline --candidate artifacts/design-feedback/candidate --output artifacts/design-feedback/comparison
npm run design:test
npx tsc --project tsconfig.design.json --noEmit
```

Open the resulting `index.html` directly in a browser; it uses relative local
files and needs no server or model. Each output must be a **new directory**.
Capture owns an in-process, loopback-only Vite server on port 1459 (override with
`--port`); it refuses busy ports, never uses Tauri's 1420, and closes its own
server/browser on success, failure or interruption. No browser is bundled with
the app and none is downloaded by capture itself.

For interactive inspection, run the normal Vite dev server and open
`/preview/design-feedback.html?scenario=conversation-long&theme=klide-light`.
Themes: `klide-light`, `sage-garden-dark`; captures use both at 1440×900 and
900×700, DPR 1. `window.__designFeedback` exposes `ready`, `scenarioId`,
`fixtureVersion`, `states`, `reset()` and `setState(name)`.
Named states are scoped to each scenario: long conversation has `earlier`;
tools/review has `diff` and `rejected`; waiting/error has `error` and `recovered`;
child activity has `settled`; all support `initial`. `composer-menu` opens its
production model picker on entry/reset. Reset restores the original model,
transcript and pending gates and clears recorded actions and drafts. Unknown
scenarios/themes/states fail explicitly. Fresh browser contexts isolate storage;
reset clears the production composer draft cache too. The capture clock fixes
Date to the fixture time while allowing real timers and interaction animations.

## Evidence and checks

A bundle contains latest/earlier PNGs, accessible YAML snapshots, automated
accessibility findings, console/page/network errors, checks, a manifest, a
source patch, untracked source inputs and a pending native-desktop checklist.
It records source/fixture/brief/file hashes, browser and platform versions,
viewport, DPR, theme, locale and timezone. Source hashing covers the declared
source/config paths in `evidence.mjs`, excluding generated artifacts and private
runtime state. Evidence is local and ignored by Git.

The patch, the copied untracked inputs and the "source changed during capture"
check cover only what was **rendered**: the files the page imported (Vite's
module graph, listed as `source.rendered`) plus the capture tooling. Another
session editing an unrelated file neither fails the run nor rides into the
bundle; an edit to a rendered file fails it and names the file.

Scenario ids, themes, sizes and the frozen clock live once, in
`catalog.json`, read by the fixture page, the capture scripts and the native
parity menu. The fixture page refuses to load if `SCENARIO_STATES` and the
catalog disagree.

The capture fails on blank root, missing fonts, unknown IPC calls, page/console
errors, external requests, document overflow, an unreachable composer or failed
interaction assertions. Every intermediate state is captured with its own
accessible snapshot and accessibility scan. Unexpected native calls fail even if production code
catches their rejection. Accessible snapshots use Playwright's `ariaSnapshot`.
The regression suite injects an overflow defect and proves the check rejects it.
Accessibility violations are preserved as findings rather than silently claimed
as passes; this slice does not enforce an existing-code accessibility baseline.

Comparisons verify file hashes and matching environments, fixture and brief
identities before showing baseline/candidate/diff images. A changed pixel is
not evidence of better design. Capture completion describes browser evidence,
not native parity or design quality. No masking is used. Still capture temporarily disables CSS animations/transitions
and caret painting, waits for rendering frames, and requires consecutive
byte-identical screenshots. The temporary stylesheet is removed before the next
interaction; a state that never settles fails capture.

## Pixel repeatability

Capture launches Chromium with fixed raster flags (`RASTER_ARGS` in
`browser.mjs`: no font hinting, no LCD text, sRGB, no runtime Skia
optimisations, no partial or GPU raster), recorded in the manifest's
environment. With them, two captures of one revision are byte-identical
(verified 2026-11-09: 20/20 `tools-and-review` stills, 0 changed pixels).

A comparison reports two counts per still: `changedPixels` (any byte moved,
`threshold: 0`) and `perceptualPixels` under the declared tolerance in
`comparison.json` (pixelmatch's default colour threshold, antialiased pixels
excluded). Both are always shown; no pixels are masked and the tolerance is
never applied silently. Neither count is a design-quality score.

The isolated Mac app has its own file-access permissions. On this machine,
opening evidence directly under Documents stalled in the OS file-open call;
verification passed after copying the same immutable bundle and verification
into `/private/tmp/klide-visual-review/` with the same relative paths and selecting
that directory as the workspace. File reads and capability lookups time out
after 20 seconds each. A timed-out OS read can remain blocked in the background;
quit the test app before retrying repeated blocked reads. No macOS privacy
permission was changed for this verification.

## Hermes Focus integration

Hermes turns without an explicit reasoning-effort selection now use `hermes acp`
over newline-delimited JSON-RPC. KIDE initializes the protocol, creates or loads
the conversation session, supplies session-specific MCP servers, selects the
model, and streams the answer and observed tool activity. Loading old history
does not render it a second time. Usage is recorded when Hermes supplies it.
The process is killed on cancellation/drop; failed prompts are never retried
automatically because a foreign tool may already have changed files.

ACP permissions go through KIDE's authenticated permission bridge. Only a
single-use option actually offered by Hermes is returned. Missing identity,
bridge failures and unsupported host operations fail closed. Loaded sessions are
returned to Hermes's asking edit mode. KIDE does not execute Hermes's tool calls
again, and these edits do not become native checkpointed DiffProposals.

The session MCP server includes `memory_search` and `memory_read`, using KIDE's
native schemas and retrieval functions. The bridge binds the Workspace; results
retain provenance and inactive-entry policy. `memory_propose` queues an evidence-backed lesson in KIDE's Memory inbox; it
requires an exact quote from a non-secret Workspace file. Proposals are never
recallable until the operator keeps them. No publication tool is exposed.

Hermes ACP currently has no reasoning-effort setter. Explicit effort selections
and generic `harness-source:` selections retain the existing CLI transport;
Hermes-specific `hermes-source:` selections support ACP. A transition through
the CLI forgets the ACP session so a later ACP turn receives the full current
conversation. Terminal/Mission sessions retain the existing CLI path. CLI session
history import and Skill proposals from Hermes remain future work.

Protocol references checked against the installed adapter and official docs:
[ACP host integration](https://hermes-agent.nousresearch.com/docs/user-guide/features/acp),
[Hermes architecture](https://hermes-agent.nousresearch.com/docs/developer-guide/architecture).

# MLX prompt-cache experiment

Klide's MLX Harness now appends a TODO snapshot when its state changes instead
of rewriting an early system message. Unchanged state adds no tokens. The
latest snapshot carries the current list, including an empty list after a
clear. Other providers retain their existing refresh behavior; local Chat
continues to omit project TODOs.

The MLX-LM launcher also sets `--prompt-cache-bytes 1GB` (supported by the
installed mlx-lm 0.31.3). This is a budget for prompt reuse, not a cap on model
weights, total process memory, or the active context window. The server trims
retained caches while admitting batched work; a large active request can still
exceed the budget. MLX-VLM is not given this MLX-LM-specific flag. Restart MLX
from Klide after rebuilding the app to apply the launch setting. Older runtimes
must support this flag; no packages are upgraded automatically.

This targets reuse **between tool turns within a run**. Resuming a conversation
reconstructs context from its transcript, and the transient TODO snapshots are
not replayed. Compaction, model changes, tool-schema changes, and server cache
eviction can still prevent reuse. Historical snapshots also add a small amount
of context each time the list changes.

## Reproduce

Export synthetic requests from the real Rust Harness loop, using the real
OpenAI adapter's wire normalization:

```sh
cd src-tauri
KLIDE_MLX_CACHE_FIXTURE=/tmp/klide-mlx-cache.json cargo test --lib mlx_todo_updates_preserve_the_processed_prefix
```

With an MLX-LM server already running, from the workspace root:

```sh
python3 -B scripts/mlx-cache/bench.py \
  --fixture /tmp/klide-mlx-cache.json \
  --output /tmp/klide-mlx-cache-results.json \
  --repeats 1
```

`default_model` means the model configured when that server started, not a
particular model family. Only use `--model` for an already-loaded model: a
server may otherwise load/download a model in response to a request. The
script does not install anything or restart the server. **Use a server with a
prompt-cache byte budget.** Unique trials retain
separate caches, which can consume several GB on an unbounded server. It accepts only
loopback HTTP endpoints, ignores proxy configuration, and refuses redirects.

## What is measured

The fixture reads a synthetic 160-line Rust file, then completes TODO T1.
`rewrite` reconstructs the previous policy from the captured request;
`append` uses the current request verbatim. During development, the
reconstruction was checked against requests captured before the code change.

Each policy gets a warm request followed by the measured next request. A fresh
nonce at the start of each sample's system prompt isolates it from other
samples. Ordering alternates between policies. Initial model warmup is excluded.
Both policies use identical tools and sampling settings (temperature zero,
thinking disabled for the experiment, eight output tokens). Klide's production
sampling settings are unchanged. One repeat makes seven requests; three repeats
make 15, including warmup and two status checks. No returned tool call is executed.

The JSON records time to first nonempty streamed delta, total request time,
prompt tokens, server-reported cached tokens, and generated text. Missing
metrics stay null. Two simple status checks ask whether T1 is complete. These
are smoke tests, **not** evidence of coding accuracy or overall task speed.
Peak memory and int8/MTP performance are not measured by this experiment.
An interrupted report is partial (`complete: false`), not a successful benchmark.

Avoid other inference workloads while benchmarking. The server's cache is used
but never cleared; sample nonces prevent reuse between trials without deleting
another conversation's cache. Normal cache eviction still applies.

Apple M5, 16 GB RAM; existing MLX-LM server's `default_model` alias. Installed

# Remote host setup

How to set up a machine Klide can run agents on. This prepares the machine
only. In Klide, Settings › Machines installs the matching native Run host
over SSH; the machine picker starts a streaming task that can survive the
Mac disconnecting. See `docs/REMOTE_MACHINES.md` for setup, verification and
remaining live acceptance.

The server runs the agent, keeps its own logins, and stays on. Your Mac only
connects to it over SSH, through Tailscale (a private network between your
devices), so the server never exposes SSH to the internet.

For an existing SSH machine, use **Settings › Machines › Add machine**:
enter its address, continue through connection and installation, sign in to
Claude on the machine, and choose or clone the remote project. You can save
the setup while the machine is off. Same-architecture Macs can use the app's
own matching executable; other targets download a checksum-verified helper.
Neither path needs GitHub CLI on the client Mac. Preparation supports Ubuntu
24.04+ / Debian 13+ x86_64, macOS on Apple silicon or Intel, and native Windows
x86_64 over OpenSSH. Windows uses PowerShell and Git for Windows, without WSL.
Unattended connections use SSH keys. See the native target details in
[Remote machines](../../docs/REMOTE_MACHINES.md).

The scripts below are an optional Linux provisioning path for creating a new server.

Provisioning files:

| File | What it does | Where it runs |
|---|---|---|
| `cloud-init.yaml` | Creates your user with your key at first boot | Pasted into the provider when you create the server |
| `bootstrap.sh` | Updates, locks down, installs git, `gh`, Node, Claude Code, Tailscale | Once on the server, over SSH |
| `bootstrap.sh --tailscale-only` | Closes public SSH once Tailscale works | Once, at the end |

The same steps rebuild the server from scratch at any time.

## 1. On the Mac, once

1. Make a key used only for this server:

   ```bash
   ssh-keygen -t ed25519 -C "mac → klide-box" -f ~/.ssh/klide_box
   ```

2. Install Tailscale on the Mac (<https://tailscale.com/download>) and sign in.
3. Fill your key into the first-boot file:

   ```bash
   cd ~/Documents/Private/KIDE
   sed "s|__SSH_PUBLIC_KEY__|$(cat ~/.ssh/klide_box.pub)|" \
     scripts/remote-host/cloud-init.yaml > ~/Desktop/klide-box-user-data.yaml
   ```

## 2. Create the server

Any provider that takes "cloud config" or "user data" works. Hetzner Cloud is
cheap and has EU data centers; DigitalOcean, OVH and Scaleway work the same way.

| Setting | Choose |
|---|---|
| Image | Ubuntu 24.04 |
| Size | 2 vCPU and 4 GB RAM or more (8 GB if it will build Rust projects) |
| Location | The one nearest you |
| SSH key | Add `~/.ssh/klide_box.pub` if the provider asks |
| Cloud config / user data | Paste the contents of `~/Desktop/klide-box-user-data.yaml` |
| Name | `klide-box` |

Note the server's public IP address.

## 3. Connect and bootstrap

Add this to `~/.ssh/config` on the Mac (create the file if needed):

```
Host klide-box
  HostName <the server's public IP>
  User pierre
  IdentityFile ~/.ssh/klide_box
  IdentitiesOnly yes
  ServerAliveInterval 30
```

Then:

```bash
cd ~/Documents/Private/KIDE
scp scripts/remote-host/bootstrap.sh klide-box:~
ssh -t klide-box 'bash ~/bootstrap.sh'
```

It ends by listing the logins left to do: Tailscale, `gh`, git identity,
Claude Code. Do them in an `ssh klide-box` session, then `sudo reboot`.

## 4. Close public SSH

1. In `~/.ssh/config`, change `HostName <public IP>` to `HostName klide-box`
   (its Tailscale name).
2. Check that `ssh klide-box` still gets in, now through Tailscale.
3. Close the public door:

   ```bash
   ssh -t klide-box 'bash ~/bootstrap.sh --tailscale-only'
   ```

   It refuses unless you are connected through Tailscale, so it can't lock you
   out. If you ever lose Tailscale, the provider's web console still reaches
   the server.

## 5. Check it works

```bash
ssh klide-box 'cd ~/code && gh repo clone pierreprudh/<some-repo> && ls'
ssh -t klide-box 'cd ~/code/<some-repo> && claude'
```

Then the survival test, which is the thing Klide will automate:

```bash
ssh -t klide-box 'tmux new -s test'      # inside: start claude, give it a task
# close the terminal window mid-task, wait a minute, then:
ssh -t klide-box 'tmux attach -t test'   # the work kept going
```

## A PC at home instead

Install Ubuntu Server 24.04 from a USB stick (server name `klide-box`, user
`pierre`, tick **Install OpenSSH server**), then from the Mac:

```bash
ssh-copy-id -i ~/.ssh/klide_box.pub pierre@<its IP>
scp scripts/remote-host/bootstrap.sh pierre@<its IP>:~
ssh -t pierre@<its IP> 'bash ~/bootstrap.sh --home'
```

`--home` adds `klide-box.local` naming on your network. Steps 4 and 5 are the same.

# Built-in spreadsheets

Open an `.xlsx` or `.sheet.json` from the file list, command palette, or a run’s Documents section. Ask the agent in Goal mode to create or revise an Excel workbook; it produces the file for you.

The Focus surface provides worksheet tabs, a cell/formula bar, keyboard navigation, basic number formats and bold, table paste, and undo/redo for cell edits. **Add to chat** appends the selected cell’s reference, input and calculated value to the active conversation draft; it does not send a message. Unsaved values are identified in that context.

**Save** writes the native `.sheet.json` workbook. **Export Excel** creates an `.xlsx` with formulas and recalculated values. When editing an imported `.xlsx`, **Save Excel copy** creates a new file and keeps the original intact: the library does not preserve every Excel feature. The export form explains this before saving. Existing destination files are never overwritten by export.

Metadata polling refreshes clean workbooks when an agent changes the file. Unsaved work is retained and an external-change banner offers a reload. Native saves compare the originally loaded bytes against disk, refusing stale writes. Reload and close ask before discarding local changes.

## Agent creation

The shared Goal-mode system prompt includes [the agent authoring guide](agent-guide.md). `write_spreadsheet` is a native Write capability: it creates or patches an `.xlsx`, recalculates with IronCalc, blocks formula errors, and exports bytes before proposing the change. `inspect_spreadsheet` is read-only and returns paginated cells, formulas, calculated values, errors and an update hash. Neither tool depends on the viewer, a shell runtime, Excel, or network access.

Write review displays a readable cell/result diff. The validated binary payload follows the same approval, rejection memory and checkpoint path as other writes. Creates never overwrite; updates require the hash obtained by inspection and recheck exact bytes at apply time. Checkpoint rollback restores original bytes and refuses to overwrite subsequent changes. Imported complex workbooks should be revised into a new file using `source_path`.

The tools are available to tool-capable providers using Kit's native harness. Independently running Codex/Claude CLI agents have their own tool registries; they do not automatically acquire these native tools. The prompt explicitly avoids claiming unavailable capabilities.

Files written through ordinary edit tools keep their change/review evidence and also appear as readable spreadsheet documents in completion cards.

## Boundaries

- Supported import: `.xlsx` and version 1 `.sheet.json`. CSV/TSV remain text; legacy `.xls` and macro-enabled `.xlsm` keep their existing external/preview route.
- Up to 50 sheets, 10,000 rows and 256 columns per sheet, and 100,000 populated cells on import. Files are capped at 20 MB at the workspace boundary; individual pastes are limited to 10,000 cells.
- Common formulas and bounded cross-sheet references recalculate locally. Unsupported formulas and cycles surface as errors; formula errors block Excel export. This is not Excel calculation parity.
- Charts, pivot tables, macros, external workbook links, dynamic arrays, and full Excel layout fidelity are outside this version. Merged cells are read-only. Renaming a referenced sheet is refused rather than breaking its formulas.
- The workbook canvas stays paper-colored in both app themes so source cell colors remain readable.

## Implementation and verification

`src/spreadsheets/workbook.ts` owns import, schema validation, editing values, calculation and export. ExcelJS, fast-formula-parser and SSF load only with the spreadsheet surface. `scripts/check-bundle-split.mjs` prevents the spreadsheet vendor chunk from returning to the startup preload list.

`src-tauri/src/agent/spreadsheet_tools.rs` owns the native IronCalc adapter, schemas live in `agent/tools.rs`, and write review/checkpoints remain in the shared harness. Agent operations are capped at 10,000 cells, 50 sheets, 5 MB compressed / 20 MB expanded and 220 KB per request.

`src-tauri/src/spreadsheet.rs` owns workspace-rooted persistence, create-only exports, conflict checks and atomic replacement for native saves.

Run `npm test`, `npm run build`, and `cargo test --manifest-path src-tauri/Cargo.toml --lib spreadsheet`. The browser fixture at `/tests/fixtures/spreadsheet.html` uses the production component with in-memory IPC for interaction and visual QA; it is not part of the production entry.

# Klide — brand and interface guidelines

Reference draft · 17 November 2026

## Decisions

- Name: **Klide**.
- Interface: **San Francisco on macOS**, selected through the native system font stack.
- Wordmark: **Inter**, independent of the interface font. Keep the existing monospace code face.
- Preserve the app's existing light and dark themes, layouts, components, spacing and behavior.
- Deep Sea and the other palette explorations are rejected as replacements for the app themes.
- Logo placement is deferred. Pierre will add it later. Preserve the supplied symbol as the source; do not redraw it or introduce replacements.

These decisions supersede the previous palette recommendations and screenshots. The research previews were temporary. The applied production change is native system typography for the UI and Inter for the wordmark; the existing theme colors, layout geometry and logo placement are preserved.

## Product character

Klide brings the code editor, terminals, coding agents, compatible model choices and change review into one workspace. Its visual character is calm, clear and capable.

Use real product views to explain the product. Describe supported behavior precisely. Do not claim universal model compatibility, universal background execution or that every workflow remains on the Mac.

Suggested descriptor: **One workspace for your coding agents.** This remains proposed copy.

## Color — preserve current themes

Use semantic tokens from `src/styles/tokens.css`, rather than placing raw hex colors in components. Keep all existing theme variants; the following values document Klide Light and the existing Midnight dark foundation, rather than creating a new theme.

### Color rules

- Light chrome stays cool grey, with white content. Do not add cream, beige or parchment surfaces.
- Existing dark themes keep their established dark surfaces and accents. Do not replace them with navy or blue-tinted panels.
- Use accents sparingly for interactions and selected states.
- Preserve semantic success, warning, error and diff colors. Keep provider logos and user content in their own colors.
- Use readable text tokens on their actual surfaces. Do not reuse a decorative or disabled tint for necessary information.
- A selected-state fill is not a sufficient keyboard focus indicator; verify focus separately.

## Typography — San Francisco UI, Inter wordmark

The UI uses `-apple-system, BlinkMacSystemFont, "SF Pro Text", "SF Pro", system-ui, sans-serif`, which selects San Francisco on macOS. Other platforms use their native system fallback. Do not bundle or redistribute the Apple system font.

The wordmark has a separate `--font-brand` token: `"Inter", var(--font-ui)`. Inter remains locally bundled for branding and offline use. Changing the interface font must not change the wordmark.

Keep the existing product type scale as the starting point:

| Role | Size | Weight |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Compact supporting text | 12px | 400 |
| Standard interface text | 13px | 400 |
| Readable body / controls | 14px | 400 or 500 |
| Subheading | 16–18px | 500 |
| Page heading | 24px | 600 |

These role/weight assignments are interface specifications; existing component hierarchy and context take precedence over blindly applying a table. Welcome and marketing display headings can remain larger where the existing layout calls for it.

Use 400 for regular copy, 500 for labels and restrained emphasis, and 600 for headings. Keep sentence case, natural letter spacing for small text and comfortable line heights. Do not introduce multiple display families.

Retain Monaspace Neon or the user's selected monospace face for code and terminals. When changing typography, check text wrapping, button width, dropdowns, headings, accents and keyboard labels at actual app sizes.

## Layout and spacing

Preserve the real application's composition: Workspace rail, Welcome split layout and pixel nature scene, Focus transcript/composer/result panels, Workbench editor and terminal, and grouped Settings. Do not substitute generic dashboard layouts for these surfaces in brand previews.

Existing Settings specifications:

- Grouped panels: **20px corner radius**.
- Controls: **12px corner radius**.
- Rows: approximately **24px padding and gaps**.
- Toggles: pill shaped.
- Fine dividers and restrained shadows.
- Section headings outside their panel.
- Page titles stand alone; add a subtitle only when useful.

For new compositions, use the proposed spacing steps **4, 8, 12, 16, 24, 32, 48, 64, 96px**. Reuse shared component spacing before introducing new measurements. Related information stays together; unrelated sections get more space.

## Controls and states

- Reuse production controls and icons.
- Give the state-relevant primary action a clear hierarchy.
- Keep chevrons functional for menus/disclosure; use full arrows for directional navigation.
- Prefer clear action labels when an icon alone is ambiguous.
- Keep keyboard access, visible focus, accessible names and expanded states.
- Use words or icons alongside color for waiting, running, failed and review states.

## Logo — placement deferred

The app and logo do not need the same typeface. **The interface uses San Francisco on macOS; the wordmark stays in Inter.** The existing Welcome text wordmark uses the separate brand token. A different wordmark face would require a later design decision. Symbol integration remains deferred.

The supplied `Group 16.png` remains the logo reference. A byte-for-byte copy is kept at `docs/brand/assets/klide-symbol-original.png`.

Do not redraw, regularize, rotate, distort or replace the symbol. Do not add it to the app during this stage. Keep the existing text branding in Inter until Pierre supplies the ready symbol and placement.

Clear space, lockup proportions, minimum sizes and vector export specifications remain unfinalized. Earlier numeric logo rules were exploration proposals, not approved requirements. Establish them against the final artwork when logo integration begins.

## Imagery

The supplied cloud and moon banners remain marketing references. Atmospheric artwork may support editorial covers and launch communications. It does not dictate the product's light or dark palette.

Preserve the existing Welcome pixel-art nature scene. Use actual rendered application components for UI previews. Clearly identify sample data and preview-only styling.

## Voice

Direct, calm and specific. Lead with what happened or what the person can do next.

- “Review changes.”
- “Choose an agent and a compatible model.”
- “Needs your approval.”
- Describe a failure and offer a relevant next action.

Avoid invented performance claims, superlatives and vague AI promises.

The existing light and dark application themes are retained. The Deep Sea previews are discarded. San Francisco is selected through the native UI font stack, while Inter is locally bundled and applied to the wordmark. Logo integration remains deferred.

## v0.6.5 — Shells, Watchers, Links (2026-09-23)

Three things the v0.6 line gained after the 0.6.4 cut. A long command no
longer has to be sat on: a Run can start a shell in the background, read what
it wrote since last time, stop it, or ask to be woken when it exits. A
delegated subagent is no longer a static line: the parent's conversation
follows the child Run live, and a worker that failed comes back as a failure.
And what an answer names is something you can reach — a URL opens in the
browser under its name, a rooted path opens in Finder, and a file of the open
project opens in a tab.

Around them, the interface pass: a context menu that behaves like a native
menu, a conversation rename that sticks, command history that reads as
history rather than a result, and a Skills modal with the same brow as every
other overlay.

The v0.6 orchestration milestone is unchanged: Missions as outcomes, budgets,
capacity, capability routing and validation contracts are still open. The macOS
bundle is still ad-hoc signed rather than Apple-notarized. This is a patch cut
on the v0.6 line, not that milestone.

### Background shells (a command that outlives the turn)

- **`run_command` can start a command instead of running it.** A foreground
  command blocks the turn and dies on a timer — 180s by default — which is
  right for `npm test` and wrong for anything that waits on the world: a
  deploy, `gh run watch`, a slow migration were killed mid-flight and reported
  as failures. `run_command(background: true)` now returns a shell id at once
  and the agent keeps working; `read_command_output(shellId)` returns only what
  was written since the last read, so a polling loop sees each line once;
  `kill_command(shellId)` stops it. The registry (`agent/background.rs`) is
  Tauri-free like the PTY host, caps each buffer at 256 KB and *reports*
  dropped bytes rather than handing back a silent gap, and marks stderr so a
  warning does not read as a result.
- **Nothing the agent started outlives the Run.** Shells are reaped in
  `settle_run`, the one terminal door every outcome passes through,
  cancellation included. Shells are run-scoped: another Run's shell id is
  indistinguishable from one that never existed, and a model that lost its own
  id gets its shells listed back so it recovers instead of doing the work
  twice.
- **Polling is its own capability.** `read_command_output` and `kill_command`
  carry a `ManageBackgroundShell` capability rather than `RunCommand`, for two
  reasons: a poll must not re-open the permission card every ten seconds, and
  a poll recorded as a command would inflate every Validation contract's
  command count.
- **A shell can wake the conversation.** A background command can ask to
  notify on exit; when it does, the conversation gets a follow-up turn with
  the result instead of waiting to be polled. The wake reads as a continuation
  of the answer that started the shell — one action row, each answer keeping
  its stats — with a finished marker on the tool-row indent and a hairline
  joining the wake to the exchange it belongs to on hover.

### Subagent watcher (a child Run you can see working)

- **The "Delegated to" line follows the child live.** `spawn_subagent` parked
  the parent and showed one static line while the child read forty files. The
  child is a Run like any other — Rust already persists its events and
  broadcasts them — so the fold now records its id (`childRunId`, from
  `subagent_requested`, so a reloaded transcript can pick a live child back
  up) and the delegation row shows its current step, step count, tokens, a
  clock, and the child's own rows on click. The same line sits under an
  `@role` background report, which previously showed a bare `· working…`.
  Settled means a real report landed, never the "Running spawn_subagent…"
  placeholder, so a running child never flashes a "View activity" button
  beside a static line, and an interrupted child stops animating.
- **A subagent inherits the parent's command timeout.** `SubagentRunSpec`
  carries `command_timeout_secs`, so a child reads the Settings value instead
  of silently falling back to 180s.

### Workers (what a child's result may claim)

- **A failed child is a failed Tool result.** Loop completion is not task
  success: a cancelled, exhausted or errored child could return `Ok` with the
  answer it wrote before stopping. A child report now counts as success only
  when its durable Run summary says `done` and it produced an answer; anything
  else returns `ok: false` to the parent with the error itself, and the result
  carries `runId` and `outcome`. Success describes execution, not an accepted
  validation contract.
- **An isolated worker reports its checkout as Git saw it.** After settlement
  the result records `headCommit`, `branch` and `hasUncommittedChanges`; a
  failed inspection is exposed as `checkoutError`, never converted to a clean
  checkout, and auto-commit stays best-effort rather than an unconditional
  "committed" claim. The worker's prose cannot certify th

# Klide

The domain language of Klide — a minimalist AI-first IDE. One context for the whole repo: the editor shell, the agent harness, and Mission Control all share these terms. Architecture reviews and design discussions use this vocabulary; when code disagrees with it, the code is what drifts.

## Core product principle: harness and model independence

Klide should let the user choose the agent runtime and the intelligence that
powers it independently: **any supported harness with any compatible model**.
The native Harness or a Delegate supplies the coding workflow and tools; the
model's Provider supplies intelligence through an API, a local server, a
self-hosted endpoint, or a subscription. Changing the intelligence source must
not silently change the selected agent runtime.

The agent picker selects the runtime. The model picker selects the intelligence
source and model for that runtime. Availability depends on the runtime's actual
capabilities, installed software, reachable endpoints, and authentication.
Adapters must expose supported combinations and explain restrictions; they must
not imply that every external CLI accepts every model.

Current implementation: the native Harness supports its registered model
Providers. Claude Code, Codex, OpenCode and Hermes have independent intelligence
source/model choices for supported combinations, persisted per Conversation.
Claude Code and Codex use Klide's loopback adapters for other API wires;
OpenCode uses provider configuration and Hermes its own backends. Unsupported
pairs stay visible with a reason; Amp chooses its own models. Remote Claude
Code over SSH/tmux does not carry routed intelligence. This is not universal
compatibility or live verification of every combination.

## Klide UI guidelines

The interface uses the native system font stack (San Francisco on macOS).
The wordmark uses locally bundled Inter through a separate brand font token.
Monaspace remains the code font. Preserve the existing light and
dark themes; the Deep Sea palette exploration was rejected. Logo integration
is deferred. The reference draft is `BRAND_GUIDELINES.md`.

Settings use rounded, grouped panels, following the Machines page and the
rounded settings reference approved by the user. This is the default Klide
visual language for new UI and future revisions of existing UI.

- Apply the light-grey and white palette across the whole app: chrome, rails
  and sidebars use #F5F6F7 (`--bg`); content, editors, terminals and panels use
  #FFFFFF (`--bg-elevated`, `--editor-bg`, `--terminal-bg`, `--bg-panel`). Use
  cool neutral borders. No beige, cream, parchment or warm off-white UI
  backgrounds, including theme variants, popovers, welcome screens and viewers.
  Keep accents for interaction and semantic information. Preserve the dark
  themes and colours belonging to user content, artwork or service logos.
- Group related settings in one panel with a 20px corner radius, a theme-aware
  panel background, a soft border and a subtle shadow. Separate rows with fine
  dividers. Keep section headings outside the panel.
- Let page titles stand alone by default. Add a subtitle only when it gives
  useful context beyond the title; avoid automatic title-and-subtitle templates.
  Keep explanations beside the specific controls they clarify.
- Give rows generous spacing (about 24px vertically and horizontally). Put the
  setting name and a muted description on the left, and its control on the
  right. Stack controls below the description when space is limited.
- Use rounded controls (12px corners), readable labels, and restrained status
  colours. Keep toggles pill-shaped. Reuse the shared Settings Panel/Row
  primitives and design tokens instead of styling each page independently.
- Use subtle chevron icons where they clarify a dropdown, submenu, or
  expandable group. They are functional affordances, not decoration: do not
  append them to every row or use the browser's filled triangle markers.
  Text controls such as Details, Hide details, Show or Hide are also suitable.
  Use full arrow icons for directional navigation or external destinations,
  rather than as substitutes for dropdown chevrons.
- Preserve keyboard access, visible focus, accessible control names and
  expanded state. Apply the same layout in light and dark themes.
- Show service logos where they help identify a connection (for example,
  Tailscale in the VPN section), with clear sections for distinct concerns.

The shared implementation is `src/components/settings/controls.tsx` and
`src/components/settings/settings.css`; Machines uses the same panel and
control radii. These guidelines take precedence over older comments describing
flat, borderless Settings sections or a blanket ban on chevrons.

## Language

### Workspace

**Workspace**:
The single folder open in Klide. Native file Tools resolve paths against it and enforce their rooted-path checks. Shell commands, terminal sessions, approved external-path operations and Remote checkouts have separate boundaries; this is not a claim that every process is unable to access files outside it.
_Avoid_: project, folder, root dir

**Workspace-rooted**:
The invariant that a path resolves inside the workspace, checked before any read or mutation. Enforced by the Workspace module (`src-tauri/src/workspace.rs`): commands and tools receive a `Workspace` value and resolve paths through it — there is no other sanctioned way to touch the filesystem from a path string.
_Avoid_: sandboxed, path-validated

### Agent execution

**Run**:
One agent working toward an outcome in the workspace, from start to done / error / aborted. Tracked on Mission Control whatever its source — Klide's own harness or a delegate.
_Avoid_: job, session, execution

**Harness**:
The Rust loop that drives a Klide-native run: provider streaming, tool dispatch, transcript writes, cancellation. There is exactly one; UI surfaces observe it, they don't reimplement it.
_Avoid_: agent loop, runner, executor

**Run host**:
The one door a Run passes through to be admitted, placed, controlled and
listed, whichever process runs its loop — the app, `klide ptyd` for a
background subscription conversation, or `klide scheduled` for a Schedule. It decides the host once (`placement`),
claims the conversation under one lock, spawns the Harness loop, writes the one
terminal event for a loop that left without settling, answers a card, and holds
the one definition of "active". Manual Conversations use the app's failure
budget whatever host runs them. Schedules dispatch from the persistent local
service and stop repeats after a failed occurrence until explicit retry. The
hosts (`TauriSupervisor`, `daemon::RunHost`) are adapters around it.
_Avoid_: second supervisor, per-host admission, remote fallback, background runner

**Schedule**:
A saved clock trigger with its own instructions, Workspace, agent/model, and
Run history, managed from Mission Control's Scheduled tab. Each occurrence starts a
fresh standalone Run through the existing Run host. One-time or fixed-interval;
repeats skip missed intervals and wait for the previous occurrence to settle.
A persistent per-user local service owns the clock on this Mac, even when
Klide is closed, while the Machine is awake and the user logged in. Overdue
work starts once after waking or logging in. A Schedule does not
preserve temporary full-auto command authority. An uncertain dispatch after
a crash requires explicit retry, so recovery never automatically repeats
possibly completed work. Cancelling a Schedule revokes future occurrences;
Stop controls a Run already launched. Schedule history keeps the Run id, due
time, start/finish times, execution target, status and error for each occurrence.
This Mac is the available target; Remote machine selection awaits VPS support.
Schedules are
independent of manual Conversations. See `docs/SCHEDULED_RUNS.md`.
_Avoid_: scheduled worker, second executor, cron daemon

**Machine**:
The computer a Run host runs on: this Mac, or a Remote machine. The app is
only ever on this Mac; what moves is where the Run's loop, shell and files
are. A Conversation's Run happens on one Machine at a time.
_Avoid_: box, host (that is the Run host, a process), environment

**Remote machine**:
A Linux computer Klide reaches over SSH — a rented server (VPS) or a spare
PC — with its own Machine logins and Remote checkout, which can stay on when
this Mac sleeps. New Claude Code Conversations use a native SSH transport to
`klide ptyd`, selected through Where it runs and configured in Settings → Machines.
The remote Run host persists events for replay and resumed streaming, owns
execution and supplies remote changes. Existing tmux Conversations retain their
terminal attachment. Remote Missions remain unsupported. See
`docs/REMOTE_MACHINES.md`, setup in `scripts/remote-host/`.
`agent/daemon_client.rs` is the local daemon client; `agent/remote_machine.rs`
owns native SSH Conversation placement and replay.
_Avoid_: cloud, VPS (one kind of Remote machine), server, remote host

**Remote checkout**:
The copy of a repository on a Remote machine, cloned once from its Git
remote. Native remote Conversations run in isolated remote worktrees; legacy
SSH/tmux sessions use the checkout directly. Its paths are remote paths,
never resolved on this Mac, and it sees only what was pushed — never this
Mac's unsaved or uncommitted work.
_Avoid_: mirror, sync, remote workspace

**Machine login**:
A credential that lives on the Machine that uses it — a CLI's subscription
login, `gh`, an API key. A Run uses the logins of the Machine it runs on;
Klide never copies one between Machines.
_Avoid_: forwarded credentials, shared secrets, key sync

**Harness contract**:
The written interface of the Harness: modes, tool capabilities, permission
rules, diff review, dynamic tools, transcript evidence, and anti-slop
expectations. `docs/HARNESS_CONTRACT.md` is the source of truth for this contract.
_Avoid_: implementation notes, rough docs

**Mode**:
The capability tier of a run — `chat` (no tools), `plan` (read-only tools), `goal` (full tools). Decided when the run starts. The picker offers two: **Plan**, and `goal` under its working name **Work**, the default. `chat` is not picked; it is what Work collapses to when the model cannot call tools.
_Avoid_: agent type, permission level, "Goal mode" (Goal is the `/goal` command now)

**Goal**:
An objective a run works toward until it is done, named with the `/goal` lede
in the composer (`/goal fix the flaky tab test`). The message goes out as
typed; the turn rides in Work whatever the picker says, and the system prompt
tells the model what the lede asks — say what done means, verify, keep going,
report. Not a Mode and not a Mission: one conversation turn with a finish line.
_Avoid_: goal mode, task (a Mission Task is a different lifecycle)

**Goal gate**:
The Harness' check on a Goal's "done": when the model stops calling tools after
changing the workspace, the configured post-edit check command runs once more.
A failure goes back to the model as the next user turn for another round
(three by default); exhausted failures end the Run in error with the check
output. Delegate CLI goals always run the configured check. A pass, no native
work, or no configured command ends the Run, with a Transcript marker saying which. Where Claude Code has a Stop hook.
_Avoid_: validation contract (that is the Mission's), reviewer (a model pass, not shipped)

**Goal policy**:
What a Work (`goal`) run does with its two review gates — `review` (every edit pauses,
commands ask), `auto` (edits apply, still checkpointed; commands ask), `full`
(edits and commands, no prompts). Chosen per conversation — the live foot bar's
note cycles it; before a conversation exists, Focus's start-stage "+" menu lists
it — stamped onto each run request, never persisted (a reload reverts to
prompting).
_Avoid_: autonomy level, trust mode, rung (the ladder is gone)

**Tool**:
A workspace-rooted capability the model can call during a run (read_file, grep, write_file…). Defined by a schema and an execution, which belong together.
_Avoid_: function, action

**Tool capability**:
The trust effect of a Tool — read workspace, write workspace, run command,
pause for user, or future network access. Modes permit capabilities; individual
Tool names do not bypass that policy.
_Avoid_: tool category, permission flag

**Permission engine**:
The Harness decision path that classifies a Tool capability against the Mode,
emits a permission request when needed, remembers per-run approvals/rejections,
and only then executes command-, network- and message-capability Tools.
_Avoid_: confirmation modal, approval UI

**Validation contract**:
The evidence snapshot derived from the Transcript that says whether a Run's
changes were diff-reviewed and command-validated. It is a guardrail against AI
slop, not a proof that the implementation is correct.
_Avoid_: test result, quality score, correctness

**Goal loop**:
A bounded supervisor contract above one or more Runs: explicit goal,
definition of done, gates, revision/stall/budget limits, and a final stop
reason. It does not execute Tools. The Harness still owns provider turns and
Tool dispatch; the Goal loop decides whether the evidence is enough to keep
going, revise, stop, or record completion.
_Avoid_: autonomous mode, background agent, second harness

**Gate**:
A falsifiable review point in a Goal loop, such as plan coverage, delivery
coverage, Diff scope, command validation, semantic review, budget, or human
approval. A failed Gate creates bounded revision work; it does not create an
unbounded retry loop.
_Avoid_: vibe check, soft review, confidence score

**Agent event**:
A typed event a run emits (token, tool call, status change). The only way any surface learns what a run is doing.
_Avoid_: message, update

**Subagent**:
A focused task a Run hands off through `spawn_subagent` and gets a report back
from. Without a worker it is read-only and runs on the parent's own model,
inside the parent's Run (explorer, reviewer). Not a Mission Task.
_Avoid_: helper, sub-task, thread

**Worker**:
A subagent handed to another agent — a Delegate CLI or a hosted API provider —
as a gated Run of its own, in its own worktree on a `klide/worker-…` branch, so
it may edit. The operator approves every dispatch on a card. Its report carries
the Git state the Harness observed, never only the worker's word.
_Avoid_: background agent (that is a *background dispatch*), bot, instance

**Side question**:
A user-invoked `/btw` Conversation beside the main Conversation. It has its
own Run, transcript, model selection and Stop, plus a bounded snapshot of the
parent's public conversation text refreshed at dispatch. It shares the parent's
Workspace for reads; Rust pins the child to read-only native Harness tools,
including after history resume. It cannot edit, run commands, dispatch Workers,
or message the main agent. Closing the panel hides it without stopping either
Run. A Side question is independent of a Subagent report or advisor consultation.
_Avoid_: second writer, advisor, Worker

**Background dispatch**:
A worker the parent does not wait for: `spawn_subagent` with `background:
true` returns the child's Run id at once, the child keeps working as a Run of
its own, and its report is delivered at a later turn boundary of the parent —
or by a follow-up turn the Harness starts for it — the way an observer
completion is. Meanwhile the parent inspects and cancels it through the
coordination verbs (`agent_list`, `agent_cancel`, `agent_read_result`). A
Mission Task is still the detached form that survives the app closing.
_Avoid_: async worker, fire-and-forget, daemon

**Run coordination**:
The Rust-owned control plane through which Runs identify, address, steer, wait
for, cancel, and return structured work to one another. Its append-only journal
under `.klide/coordination/` is shared across private worktrees and folds into a
snapshot; the Harness, Delegate adapters, UI, embedded MCP, and future local
socket are consumers of this one domain, never competing coordinators.
_Avoid_: terminal orchestration, agent chat, external A2A provider, panel routing

**Coordination bridge**:

**Coordination bridge**:
The app-process loopback door through which a Delegate CLI's embedded MCP
server reaches Run coordination. It binds the calling Run's identity and
Workspace from the PTY session Klide spawned — never from a request field —
accepts a call on a session's line only with that session's own secret, and
forwards each operation to the journal's single writer gate, so a Delegate
and a Harness Run share one authority and one change event.
_Avoid_: MCP proxy, agent API, second journal writer, remote coordination endpoint

**Coordination operation**:
One of the five things a Run does on the journal — list, send, wait, cancel,
read result — as a single core function that takes an actor a door already
authenticated and returns one structured result rendered as one text. A door
(the Harness's native Tools, the Delegate bridge) binds the actor and wraps
the reply; it never decides what the operation does. One schema source lists
the five for both doors.
_Avoid_: bridge op, tool handler, per-door implementation, MCP tool (as the definition)

**Coordination envelope**:
A durable semantic payload addressed from an operator or authenticated Run to
one stable Run id. It has an explicit kind, correlation/reply identity,
idempotency key, evidence references, and queued → delivered → acknowledged
lifecycle. Delivery happens at an execution adapter's safe boundary; terminal
bytes are never the authoritative envelope. A reply reverses the route it
answers: only the original recipient may answer the original sender with that
envelope's reply identity, so an id is an address, never an entry pass. A
Run's reply is kind answer, and one per envelope; anything more is a new,
reviewed message.
_Avoid_: Agent event, prompt injection, terminal text, chat message

**Delivery**:
Everything a Run's model reads that the operator did not type — peer
envelopes and background observer completions — rendered once, in front of the
operator's own words, with each item inside a fence closed by a per-delivery
random nonce. A body cannot close its fence, so nothing inside one can pose as
Klide's framing or speak for the operator. The same renderer serves the turn
boundary, `agent_wait`, a send receipt's replies, and the Delegate bridge.
_Avoid_: inbox text, injected message, system note

**Send receipt**:
What a Run learns about a message it just sent: the envelope's delivery state
read back from the journal, and — reported separately — whether this call
waited for a reply and got one. Both are observations of durable state, so a
retry that appended nothing and a wait that timed out are described rather than
disguised; a receipt never changes the message it reports on.
_Avoid_: send result, ack, delivery promise, retry status

**Coordination result**:
The single structured outcome a Run publishes for its coordinator: status,
summary, artifacts, and evidence references. A result reports work; reviewed
knowledge extracted from it may later become Project Memory, but the result
itself is not memory.
_Avoid_: last assistant message, terminal tail, memory entry

**Coordination snapshot**:
The replay-derived view of registered Runs, normalized states, cancellation
requests, envelope delivery, and results at one journal cursor. Consumers take
a snapshot and then read events from `nextSeq`; React state and focused panels
never become the source of truth.
_Avoid_: agent registry, live panel list, cached bus state

**Document**:
A file a Run produced or referenced that a person opens rather than reads as a
diff — a workbook, a PDF, a deck. Listed on the completion card as something to
open; a reference recovered from an older transcript is shown as a reference,
never as an edit the Run made.
_Avoid_: output file, attachment, deliverable

**Workbook**:
An `.xlsx` or `.sheet.json` Klide recalculates and opens itself. Written by the
`write_spreadsheet` Tool (created or patched, recalculated and exported before
review) and read by `inspect_spreadsheet`; its bytes travel as the binary
payload of an ordinary DiffProposal, so approval, rejection memory, checkpoint
and rollback are the same ones every edit gets.
_Avoid_: Excel file, sheet (the file), xlsx blob

**Sheet surface**:
Klide's built-in workbook editor — worksheet tabs, formula bar, keyboard
navigation, paste, undo, and Add to chat. Local recalculation of common
formulas, not Excel parity; the limits are written down in
`src/spreadsheets/README.md`.
_Avoid_: spreadsheet viewer, grid, Excel mode

**Retained value**:
A tool result too large to carry in the provider messages, written once to the
Run's value store and shown to the model as a stub with a head/tail preview;
`peek_value` reads slices on demand. The Transcript still records the full
result, so replay rebuilds the same stub.
_Avoid_: truncated output, cached result

**Transcript**:
The append-only JSONL record of a run's agent events on disk. A run can be replayed from it.
_Avoid_: log, history, chat history

**Conversation**:
The reader-facing shape of a Transcript. There is one owner of the wire format,
`src/agent/foldEvents.ts`: `createFold` folds an Agent event stream into
`FoldedRow[]`, at two paces over the same code — replay drains a whole
transcript (`foldAgentEvents`), and the live run feeds it one event at a time
through the AI panel's turn driver. Two mappers project the rows into the two
shapes surfaces actually render — `Msg[]` for the AI panel, `RunMessage[]` for
Mission Control. Everything downstream is a projection of that fold, never a
second parse of the events.

Two further folds sit *on top* of it, and are views rather than parsers:
`src/transcripts.ts
…[仅保留首 16KB/中段 8KB/末 8KB]…
ness itself. A compatible selection can be an API key, local/self-hosted
endpoint, or subscription inference service. A subscription CLI is not by
itself an inference endpoint. Nous Portal exposes one through Hermes's official
subscription proxy; Klide's Messages and Responses adapters let Claude Code
and Codex consume compatible inference, while OpenCode uses its native provider
configuration. Capability checks decide which pairs run, and unsupported pairs
remain visible with their missing adapter explained. Selecting a source never
silently switches the Harness. Conversation routing records source, model, and
an optional per-run effort override; the process host resolves credentials.
Effort choices follow the source's model capabilities. Provider default omits
the override; routed bridges translate an explicit choice into the provider's
wire format. Unknown effort controls stay hidden.

**Provider catalog**:
The Rust registry as the renderer reads it — every row published as plain
data (`ai_list_providers`), mirrored into
`src/agent/providerCatalog.generated.ts` by a Rust test that fails when the
mirror is stale, and read through one TS door
(`src/agent/providerCatalog.ts`). The picker's rows, the API-keys list, the
local-server rows and the default-model fallbacks are all derived from it.
`auto` and `custom:*` / `cli:*` ids are not rows; the door answers for them
explicitly rather than with a builtin's value.
_Avoid_: provider list, provider table, PROVIDER_CATALOG (that is the
picker's derived view, not the catalog)

**Auto**:
The Provider the picker sends when the user leaves the model choice to Klide.
Not a backend: the Harness router (`src-tauri/src/agent/routing.rs`) replaces
it with a concrete Provider + model at run start, and `RunStarted` carries the
resolved pair, so every surface shows what actually ran. The rule is: rule out
what cannot do the job (no key, server down, no tools when the Mode needs
them, a window the prompt won't fit); prefer starred models nearest the
task's Rung, cheapest first, then each keyed Provider's ladder model for that
Rung and what is installed locally; lock the pick for the conversation — a
continuation reuses its origin, never routes again. `RouteResolved` records
the reason and what was ruled out. Distinct from the Goal policy's `auto`
(edits apply without review): that is a review setting, this is a Provider.
_Avoid_: smart mode, auto-select, model router (the router is the mechanism;
Auto is the choice the user makes)

**Rung**:
How much model a task shape asks for: `light`, `standard` or `strong`. Read
off the request in `rung_for` (`src-tauri/src/agent/routing.rs`) — Chat is
light, Plan and Goal are standard, a big first turn bumps one up — never off
a model call. A hosted Provider row names one model per Rung (its
`AutoLadder`; local and subscription rows have `NO_LADDER`), an installed
local model sits at light, and the nearest Rung with a passing candidate
answers when the wanted one has none. The declared rule is the prior any
learned signal would have to beat.
_Avoid_: tier (that is the Mission planner's cost tier), level (reasoning
effort), difficulty score (it is three steps, not a number)

**Model capabilities**:
The one answer to what a model can do — context window, tools, vision,
reasoning levels, price class, maker — for one Provider + model pair
(`src-tauri/src/model_capabilities.rs`). Resolved in one order: explicit
override → provider metadata (a CLI's manifest, a `/models` listing, a
registry row) → local probe (Ollama's `/api/show`) → name table; memoised per
pair. The gauge, the router, the compaction threshold and the composer
controls all read the same answer, so they cannot disagree. A window nobody
published is unknown (`null`), not a default. The price class is decided by
the Provider (subscription flag, `KeySource`), never by the model's name.
_Avoid_: per-command heuristics, frontend fallbacks, model metadata (the
listing is a source; this is the answer)

### Mission Control

**Mission Control**:
The board aggregating every run in the workspace — Klide convos and delegate tasks side by side — with observe / take over / stop controls.
_Avoid_: dashboard, agent panel

**Run inspection**:
The resolved detail subject for one Mission Control selection. It prefers a
durable Transcript over its live Klide convo twin, supplies live messages only
until that Transcript lands, and resolves fork lineage around the same Run.
_Avoid_: selected row state, detail-pane data

**Task**:
A queued todo on Mission Control. Starts as a plain item; "send an agent" dispatches a delegate to work on it. A task is the intent, the run is the work.
_Avoid_: ticket, issue, todo

**Delegate**:
An external CLI agent (Claude Code, Codex, OpenCode, Oh My Pi) dispatched into the workspace through a PTY session. Klide observes its output; it does not drive its loop. All per-CLI knowledge lives in the Delegate module (`src-tauri/src/delegate/`), one adapter per CLI: spawn syntax, resume flags, session-id detection, transcript parsing — and the CLI's *facts*: its label and binary, its login commands and auth check, whether its login can be switched (`supports_accounts`), and its **home** — the config and data directories honouring the CLI's own override (`CODEX_HOME`, `CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR`, XDG for OpenCode) and the paths under them (sessions, the config file Klide writes hooks into, auth files, model cache). Every other module asks the adapter for a path; none spells `~/.codex` itself (a source scan in `delegate/home.rs` enforces it). Resolution reads through an `Env` so a test can move a home without touching the process.
_Avoid_: external agent, subprocess, CLI tool

**Delegate catalog**:
The Delegate facts a surface shows without spawning one — id, label, binary, `supportsAccounts` — as `delegate::catalog()` in Rust, mirrored verbatim in `src/delegates.ts` (the frontend's one source: the `DelegateId` union, `delegateLabel`, every label map and the account-switcher flag derive from it) and served live by `delegate_catalog`. The Rust test `frontend_catalog_matches_all` pins the mirror to the adapters; a vitest source scan pins the rest of `src/` to the mirror.
_Avoid_: delegate list, provider table

**Klide convo**:
A snapshot of an AI-panel conversation published to Mission Control, so it stays on the board after its panel closes.
_Avoid_: chat, conversation, thread

**Account snapshot**:
A saved copy of the credentials a Delegate CLI already wrote, captured so Klide can switch which account that CLI runs under (personal vs. work). Snapshot/restore only — Klide never mints or refreshes tokens. Stored under `~/.klide/accounts/<provider>/`.
_Avoid_: login, credential, token

**Account provider**:
The per-CLI seam for Account snapshots (`src-tauri/src/accounts.rs`) — one `AccountProvider` backend per CLI whose Delegate says `supports_accounts` (Codex / Claude Code / OpenCode) behind a trait. A backend names its Delegate and reads the CLI's id, label, login command and login files from that adapter — it keeps no id list, label or path of its own; what stays here is how to read the identity, and how to capture and restore it. The generic save / list / activate flow knows nothing CLI-specific.
_Avoid_: account manager, credential handler

### Prompt assembly

**Library**:
The one destination for what Kit brings into every Run: Project Memory (what
it knows), Skills (how it works) and Foundations (the working notes a set of
Conversations shares). One sidebar row, one window, a tab for each. The row
speaks only when Memory has drafts waiting for review.
_Avoid_: knowledge base, context (that is the Lens), settings

**Skill**:
A user-authored prompt extension injected into a run's system prompt when active.
_Avoid_: plugin, extension, preset

**Lens**:
The auto-selected slice of project context (open file, related files, workspace landmarks) appended to a prompt. Scored per message; capped small.
_Avoid_: context tray, project context, RAG

**Diff review**:
The accept/reject gate a run's file edits pass through before landing in the workspace.
_Avoid_: approval, confirmation

colors:

  charcoal:        "#1c1c1c"   # Primary text, headings, dark CTA fills
  charcoal-83:     "rgba(28, 28, 28, 0.83)"   # Strong secondary text
  charcoal-82:     "rgba(28, 28, 28, 0.82)"   # Body copy
  charcoal-40:     "rgba(28, 28, 28, 0.40)"   # Interactive borders, button outlines
  charcoal-4:      "rgba(28, 28, 28, 0.04)"   # Subtle hover backgrounds, micro-tints
  muted:           "#5f5f5d"   # Secondary text, descriptions, captions
  # Accent (soft sage — chosen to avoid the AI-blue convention)
  accent:         "#5A7B4C"   # Primary interactive accent
  accent-soft:    "rgba(90, 123, 76, 0.12)"   # Subtle accent tint
  accent-hover:   "#6B8E5A"   # Accent on hover (slightly brighter). Every theme must set this:

principles:
  - "Page titles stand alone by default. Use subtitles only for useful additional context; place specific explanations beside the controls they clarify."
  - "Light grey and white throughout. Chrome is #F5F6F7; content is #FFFFFF. No beige, cream, parchment or warm off-white UI backgrounds."
  - "Sage over blue. The accent is a soft sage green (#5A7B4C) — every AI tool defaults to blue; we don't."
  - "Charcoal over black. Text is #1c1c1c, not #000. The slight off-black reads as organic, not digital."
  - "Opacity grays over hex grays. Every gray is the same charcoal at a different transparency. Tonal coherence is automatic."
  - "Soft borders and subtle shadows contain rounded groups. Keep dividers fine and spacing generous."
  - "Selection is a grey lift, not a colour. Picked rows in lists and menus (Explorer, Git Review files, Where it runs) fill with the text colour at ~10% and hover at ~5%, on 8px corners — never the accent."
  - "San Francisco for the macOS interface; Inter for the wordmark. Keep the current light and dark themes."
  - "Monaspace over JetBrains. Code gets a different typeface. Same warmth, but mechanical."
  - "Restrained emphasis. Preserve existing component hierarchy and use stronger weights only where useful."

# ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# KNOWN GAPS
# ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

known_gaps:
  - "Form input error states — focus ring is documented, but validation error styles are not."
  - "Decorative gradients — any chrome gradients must stay neutral grey/white in light themes; artwork retains its own palette."
  - "Chart tokens — --chart-1..7 ship in tokens.css but are not documented here."
  - "Context-window tokens (--ctx-messages, --ctx-tools, --ctx-system, --ctx-skills, --ctx-rules, --ctx-lens, --ctx-draft, --ctx-reply) are a sanctioned hue exception, like the git lanes: one soft pastel per kind of token so the 7px breakdown bar's segments can be told apart. Hovering a segment or row lights that kind and drops the others to low opacity. The context popover only — never UI chrome."
  - "Diff tokens are the one deliberate exception to the brand palette: classic code-review green/red (GitHub's #1A7F37 / #CF222E light, #3FB950 / #F85149 dark) so a diff reads the same as in every editor. --diff-add / --diff-remove colour signs, counts and edge markers; --diff-*-bg tints a changed line and --diff-*-word its changed span, both translucent so they sit on any surface."

  guided installer; cache a chosen helper while the destination is offline.
- [x] Add native Linux / both Mac architectures / Windows CI. Gate helper
  publication on runtime replay and installer checks; Windows also tests real
